chunks: "UART is asynchronous. There is no clock wire between the two devices.
Each one has its own oscillator, and they just agree beforehand on a baud rate, say 115200, so they both know how long a bit lasts.
The catch is that two independent clocks are never exactly equal and have no phase relationship, so the receiver has no idea where bits start.
That's why every byte is framed with a start bit and a stop bit.
The start bit is a falling edge that tells the receiver 'now', and from that edge it counts its own bit times and samples each bit in the middle.
At the next byte it re-syncs from the next start edge, so errors don't pile up.

Contrast that with SPI or I2C, which are synchronous: a clock wire runs alongside the data, and the receiver samples exactly on the clock edges, so the two sides can't drift relative to each other, and the speed is just whatever the clock is.
The trade is that async saves a wire and tolerates unrelated clocks, but costs framing overhead, 20% at 8N1, and needs the two baud rates to match within a few percent.
One footnote: many chips are USARTs, which can also run in a synchronous mode with a clock pin, but plain UART use is asynchronous."
